reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India NTEP
clinicalPearls: A chronic granulomatous subcutaneous infection characterised by the triad of painless swelling, multiple discharging sinuses and extrusion of grains, most often affecting the foot
It is either eumycetoma, caused by true fungi, or actinomycetoma, caused by aerobic filamentous bacteria such as Nocardia and Actinomadura, and this distinction dictates treatment
Grain colour offers a clue to aetiology: black grains suggest fungal causes, while red, yellow or white grains suggest actinomycetes
It is a neglected tropical disease of barefoot agricultural workers, endemic in the 'mycetoma belt' including parts of India, and follows traumatic inoculation
Disease spreads locally to involve subcutaneous tissue, fascia and bone, causing deformity and disability, but rarely disseminates systemically
Diagnosis combines grain microscopy and culture, histopathology, imaging for bone involvement and increasingly molecular identification of the causative organism
Actinomycetoma responds to prolonged combination antibacterial therapy, whereas eumycetoma requires prolonged antifungal therapy often combined with surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Following traumatic inoculation of soil-dwelling fungi or aerobic actinomycetes, the organisms aggregate into grains (microcolonies) within subcutaneous tissue. The host mounts a suppurative and granulomatous response, forming abscesses and sinus tracts that discharge grains to the surface. Chronic inflammation and progressive spread involve fascia, muscle and bone, producing swelling, fibrosis, deformity and osteolysis. The grain structure and, in eumycetoma, a surrounding cement substance protect organisms from host defences and antimicrobials, accounting for the chronicity and treatment difficulty.
infectionMimics: Tuberculosis of bone and soft tissue
additionalInvestigations: Examination of discharged grains for colour, and microscopy after potassium hydroxide or staining
Culture of grains to distinguish fungal from actinomycetous causes
Histopathology of deep biopsy showing grains within granulomatous inflammation
Imaging (radiography, ultrasound or MRI) to assess bone and soft-tissue extent
Molecular identification of the causative species where available
redFlags: Bone involvement with extensive osteolysis threatening limb function
Secondary bacterial infection or sepsis complicating chronic sinuses
Rapid progression or atypical features suggesting malignancy
reference.prognosis: Actinomycetoma generally responds well to prolonged combination antibacterial therapy, whereas eumycetoma is often refractory, requires prolonged antifungals with surgery and has a higher relapse rate; late presentation with bone disease may necessitate amputation.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish eumycetoma from actinomycetoma, leading to inappropriate therapy
Missing bone involvement by not imaging adequately
Delaying referral until advanced disease limits options to amputation
management: Identify and characterise the grains (microscopy, culture, molecular typing) to separate eumycetoma from actinomycetoma, as aetiology dictates the entire treatment strategy
Treat actinomycetoma with prolonged combination antibacterial therapy, typically co-trimoxazole paired with an aminoglycoside such as amikacin or with rifampicin, given in cycles
Treat eumycetoma with prolonged oral azole antifungals such as itraconazole (or newer triazoles), combined with surgery to remove the fungal focus
Undertake surgical debridement or wide local excision of localised lesions, reserving amputation for advanced disease with extensive bone destruction and disability
Provide supportive wound care of discharging sinuses, analgesia, and treatment of any secondary bacterial infection
Monitor treatment response and bone involvement with serial ultrasound or MRI, and actively support adherence given the very long treatment duration
Refer for multidisciplinary care (infectious diseases, surgery, dermatology) and promote protective footwear to prevent traumatic inoculation in endemic communities
